title: Rate Sculpting & Key Routing Strategy - Summit Finance (demo)
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood rate-sculpting features, org/project key routing, console controls, and Optimize recommendations. Discussed cost/latency tradeoffs and secure VPC deployment considerations. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot that includes a spike test and a security questionnaire follow-up.
next_steps: Redwood: send pilot plan + pricing workbook by 2026-12-03
Customer: provide sample traffic profile and list of top 20 API keys by 2026-12-06
Schedule pilot kickoff (stack + IAM review) for week of 2026-12-08
action_items: Maya Chen: share console walkthrough recording and quota templates (due 2026-12-03)
Leo Alvarez: prepare a synthetic spike test script and baseline latency spreadsheet (due 2026-12-04)

transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~51 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Leo Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jon Park (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Summit Finance), Ethan Moore (SRE), Lina Park (Security), Ravi Menon (APIs)

[00:00:05] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:12] Priya Shah: Priya here, hi.
[00:00:14] Ethan Moore: Ethan on the line.
[00:00:16] Lina Park: Lina.
[00:00:18] Ravi Menon: Ravi.
[00:00:20] Maya Chen: Awesome. So today we want to show how Redwood can shape rates at org and project level, how you can use routing rules in the console to prefer cheaper model variants for non-critical flows, and some Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization — and then propose a short pilot. Is that right, Leo?
[00:00:36] Leo Alvarez: Yep, that's the plan. I'll jump into the console and show a couple config patterns — sorry if the font is tiny, I have a bunch of tabs open.
[00:00:44] Jon Park: Quick note I added the pilot deck link in the chat — there should be a baseline benchmark sheet too.
[00:00:50] Priya Shah: Great, thanks. Our main concerns are predictable latency during payroll spikes, cost controls across business units, and keeping keys tied to teams so security/audit is clear.
[00:01:02] Maya Chen: Perfect scope. Can you walk through your current stack briefly, Ravi?
[00:01:08] Ravi Menon: Sure. We run a mix: customer-facing UI calls hit an API gateway that fans out to microservices. We use per-team API keys in the gateway, then route to a shared inference cluster on prem for PII-sensitive requests. We do have cloud endpoints for lower-sensitivity batch jobs. The problem is when one team goes crazy with experiments we see tail latency and cost spikes.
[00:01:30] Ethan Moore: And the SRE ask is to avoid noisy neighbors and have hard quotas per project or team, not just org-wide.
[00:01:38] Maya Chen: Totally. Redwood supports both org-level and project-key scoped quotas. Let me show the console:
[00:01:44] [00:01:44] Leo Alvarez: (shares screen) This is the Projects view — you can define Project keys that are namespaced under an Org. Each key has a concurrency limit, token quota, and per-minute rate.
[00:01:58] [00:01:58] Leo Alvarez: Here's an example: we created a "payroll-service" project key with a burst lane allowed of 500 tokens per minute, but a sustained rate of 100 tokens per minute, with auto-throttle to 80% if latency exceeds 350 ms.
[00:02:12] Priya Shah: Auto-throttle to 80% — is that a hard throttle or graceful backoff?
[00:02:16] Leo Alvarez: It's graceful — we can configure the behavior: immediate 429, leaky-bucket smoothing, or slow-start fallback to cheaper model variant.
[00:02:25] Lina Park: Can we log every 429 and tie it to the original API key for audits?
[00:02:29] Leo Alvarez: Yes, audit logs show key id, org, project, model variant used, latency bucket, and reason for rejection. Those logs are exported to your SIEM or S3.
[00:02:37] Priya Shah: Good. For the on-prem sensitive flows, do we still use the same policy engine? We want consistent behavior across private and hosted.
[00:02:45] Jon Park: Yes, same control plane can push policies to Redwood Private deployment — routing, quotas, and audit hooks are consistent. There's a handshake for local policy enforcement.
[00:02:54] Ethan Moore: What's the SLA if we put a critical service on Dedicated vs Hosted?
[00:02:58] Maya Chen: Dedicated gives you a committed GPU pool with SLA-backed latency and availability. Hosted is still fast but subject to multi-tenant scheduling — we provide latency percentiles and fallbacks.
[00:03:08] Priya Shah: Let's dig into routing rules — can we prefer cheaper models for non-sensitive endpoints and failover to higher-cost model if quality drop detected?
[00:03:16] Leo Alvarez: Yes — routing rules are policy objects. You can define a route with selectors like headers, org/project id, or path, and then an ordered list of model variants with conditions. We also support automatic canary: route 90% to cheaper quantized variant and 10% to full-precision; the platform runs quality checks on your eval set and can auto-roll back.
[00:03:34] Ravi Menon: How do we measure quality? We have a small prompt set for payroll approvals.
[00:03:38] Jon Park: Optimize integrates with your eval suite. You can upload prompts and Redwood will run A/B comparisons across variants and report BLEU-like diffs, hallucination rate, and latency/cost delta. It's not perfect but it flags regressions.
[00:03:51] Priya Shah: Is that A/B run live on production traffic or synthetic?
[00:03:54] Leo Alvarez: Can be both. We do shadow mode where we mirror requests to the candidate model and compare outputs offline. For sensitive data you can keep evaluation on-prem.
[00:04:03] Lina Park: Shadowing sensitive requests is a no for us — need on-prem eval only. Is that supported?
[00:04:07] Maya Chen: Yep. Private deployment supports on-prem eval and audit-only logs.
[00:04:12] [00:04:12] Ethan Moore: On quotas: can we have hierarchical quotas — org-level quota and project-level overrides?
[00:04:18] Leo Alvarez: Absolutely. You can set a global org monthly token cap and then carve project-level allocations. We also support borrowing rules — unused project tokens can be reallocated to a pool for other projects during low usage windows, with sticky routing so teams keep their favorites.
[00:04:33] Priya Shah: That borrowing is interesting. How do you prevent a noisy team from draining the pool during a spike?
[00:04:38] Leo Alvarez: You set burst lanes and per-key burst budgets. Once burst budget exhausted, requests hit the next policy: either queued, rate-limited, or routed to fallback model. There's also a short-circuit flag for critical routes that never fall back.
[00:04:50] Ravi Menon: Can rate-limiting be enforced at API gateway layer by Redwood, or do we need to enforce in our gateway?
[00:04:57] Jon Park: You can choose — Redwood can act as the authoritative throttle via the API, or you can push enforcement decisions to your gateway using callbacks/webhooks. For lower latency, many customers keep enforcement local and use Redwood for telemetry and policy updates.
[00:05:10] Priya Shah: Latency concerns — if we do local enforcement and talk to Redwood only for reporting, we still need prefix cache and KV cache behavior across calls, right?
[00:05:19] Leo Alvarez: Correct. Our runtime supports prefix/KV cache sharing across requests on the serving pool. For sticky routing (i.e., same session pinned to a serving node), we support session affinity via project key. That reduces warm-start costs and latency.
[00:05:33] Ethan Moore: About cost: how much does quantized variant lower token cost? Any ballpark?
[00:05:38] Maya Chen: Typical reductions are 2-4x per-token cost depending on quantization level and hardware. Optimize will estimate based on your average sequence lengths.
[00:05:46] Lina Park: Security: does Redwood store PII by default in logs?
[00:05:50] Jon Park: No — by default we hash or redact inputs for logs and you can opt into raw logging if needed for debugging, but we recommend using on-prem or VPC with KMS. Audit logs contain metadata but not raw inputs unless explicitly enabled.
[00:06:02] Priya Shah: Good. Can we tie policies to SAML groups so only certain teams can create high-priority keys?
[00:06:08] Leo Alvarez: Yes: RBAC integrates with your SSO. You can scope key creation to roles and mute some routes for lower-tier users.
[00:06:15] Ravi Menon: Ok, show us a failure scenario — what happens when the payroll-service hits a spike beyond burst budget?
[00:06:20] Leo Alvarez: (switches demo) Here's a synthetic spike runner. We set concurrency spikes to 800 rps. Watch the quota meter — once burst budget hits zero, requests are throttled and routed to fallback variant. You can see live telemetry: token burn, 429s per key, and a rolling latency percentile.
[00:06:36] [00:06:36] (audio glitch)
[00:06:38] Ethan Moore: Sorry, I'm on mobile, missed a bit.
[00:06:39] Maya Chen: No problem. The key point — you can set a grace policy so critical routes get queued and later processed rather than outright rejected. That helps jobs like payroll that must process eventually.
[00:06:49] Priya Shah: Queueing increases tail latency though — we need an SLA that limits queued time.
[00:06:53] Jon Park: You can set max queue time and also enforce deadlines. If the job expires, we revert to alerting and optional compensation flow.
[00:07:00] Lina Park: For compliance we need proof of who approved fallbacks. Is there an approval audit path?
[00:07:05] Leo Alvarez: Yes — routing rules and manual overrides are recorded with actor identity and timestamp. If you have SSO, that maps to user id.
[00:07:12] Priya Shah: About the pilot: we want Redwood to simulate a payroll-week-like spike with our traffic pattern and measure 99th percentile latency and percent of outputs hitting cheaper model variants.
[00:07:22] Maya Chen: That's doable. Our pilot will include a staged load test: baseline on your current cluster, then route same traffic through Redwood-hosted policies and measure cost delta and latency. We'll also run Optimize to recommend batch sizes and quantization levels.
[00:07:34] Ravi Menon: For the spike test, can you simulate a mixed workload — some long sequences for doc generation and many short requests for auth tokens?
[00:07:41] Leo Alvarez: Yep, our synthetic runner supports multi-template workloads with distributions. We'll use your supplied traffic profile.
[00:07:47] Ethan Moore: Any network egress concerns for sensitive payloads?
[00:07:50] Jon Park: For private deployment you can avoid egress; for hosted, we recommend tokenization at gateway and keep PII out of requests. We also support customer-managed KMS keys so logs are encrypted at rest.
[00:08:00] Lina Park: Do you do periodic penetration testing of the console and control plane?
[00:08:04] Maya Chen: Yes, we publish pen test results for enterprise customers under NDA and we have SOC2 Type II.
[00:08:11] Priya Shah: Ok, quick product question: can we programmatically create project keys when onboarding a new team?
[00:08:17] Leo Alvarez: Absolutely — there's an API and Terraform provider. You can automate key creation, attach initial quotas, and set up alerts.
[00:08:24] Priya Shah: Nice. How do alerts work? We want to be notified when a key approaches its monthly cap.
[00:08:28] Jon Park: Alerts are webhook/email/Slack channels. You can set threshold-based alerts (percent of cap) and anomaly detection alerts based on sudden deviation.
[00:08:36] Ethan Moore: Any nuance on billing when borrowing tokens between projects?
[00:08:41] Maya Chen: Billing ties back to org and project tags. For reserved capacity you'll get committed usage pricing, and overshoot is charged at pay-as-you-go. We can model the most common scenarios in the pricing workbook.
[00:08:52] Priya Shah: Okay. A few more quick clarifications: 1) can we enforce country-level routing for data residency? 2) what's the RTO for fallback?
[00:09:00] Leo Alvarez: 1) Yes, region selectors let you route to regional endpoints. 2) RTO depends on your policy — fallbacks are immediate; if you need higher durability we recommend Dedicated nodes with autoscale.
[00:09:10] Priya Shah: Great. Any competitors we should look at for reference?
[00:09:13] Maya Chen: Some customers evaluate in-house endpoints and cloud-managed inference from big clouds. It comes down to operational cost and control.
[00:09:19] Ravi Menon: Alright, this was useful. What do you need from us to start the pilot?
[00:09:24] Maya Chen: Sample traffic profile, list of critical routes and keys, and access to run a short webhook-based integration test. We'll draft the pilot SOW and send pricing.
[00:09:33] Priya Shah: We'll get that over. One ask — can you include a section in the SOW about data handling during the pilot (redaction, on-prem evaluation)?
[00:09:40] Maya Chen: Will do.
[00:09:42] Jon Park: I'll follow up with the benchmark sheet and a synthetic runner link.
[00:09:46] Ethan Moore: Thanks all.
[00:09:48] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — recap in the chat, and we'll send next steps.

Summary / Closing Notes:
- Agreed pilot: 2-week spike and routing pilot focusing on payroll workflows; Redwood to provide benchmark sheet and synthetic runner.
- Security: Summit prefers on-prem eval for PII, Redwood to include explicit data handling clause in SOW.
- Action items assigned (see action_items).

Transcript quality notes: medium — a couple audio glitches and one timestamp overlap. Some product names autocorrupted in live captions (e.g., "leaky bucket" transcribed as "lucky bucket").
